procedural_history.originating_court: Magistrate, 1st Class (commitment orders) and Assistant Sessions Judge (proceedings)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 16, 1968, of the Patna High Court dismissing Criminal Revision Nos. 345 and 346 of 1968 and Criminal Misc. Nos. 248 and 249 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Revisions Nos. 345 and 346 of 1968 in the Patna High Court against the orders of the Sessions Judge declining to quash the commitment proceedings and to make a reference to the High Court in the two Sessions Cases against the appellant. He also filed Criminal Miscellaneous Petitions Nos. 248 and 249 of 1968 to quash the orders of the Magistrate, 1st Class to stand his trial for offences under Sections 167, 466 and 471 of the Penal Code. The High Court rejected both the Criminal Revisions and the Criminal Miscellaneous Petitions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the common order of the Patna High Court. The Supreme Court confirmed the order of the High Court and dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Magistrate to take cognizance of the complaint was barred by the provisions of Section 195(1)(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: The appellant was charged with offenses under sections 167, 466, and 471 of the Penal Code.
The appellant argued that the Magistrate lacked jurisdiction to take cognizance of the complaint.

The basis for this argument was that the complaint was not filed by the appropriate court, which the appellant claimed was a mandatory requirement under Section 195(1)(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
law: Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure limits a Magistrate's power to take cognizance of certain offenses.
Section 195(1)(b) bars cognizance of certain offenses (like Section 193) unless there is a complaint from the relevant court.
Section 195(1)(c) bars cognizance of offenses like forgery (Section 471) when the offense is alleged to have been committed "by a party to any proceeding in any court".
application: The Court analyzed each charge against the appellant to see if the bar in Section 195 applied.

For the charge under Section 167, the Court rejected the appellant's claim that this was a device to evade the bar applicable to Section 193. It agreed with the High Court that the charge was justified, and noted that Section 167 is not covered by Section 195(1)(b) or (c).
For the charge under Section 466, the Court stated that this offense is "admittedly, not covered" by Section 195(1)(b) or (c).

For the charge under Section 471, the Court acknowledged that this offense is listed in Section 195(1)(c). However, it found that the bar did not apply because the appellant was not a "party" to the original proceedings. He was the presiding Magistrate in those proceedings (transfer applications) and had no personal interest in their outcome. Therefore, a crucial condition for the bar was not met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, concluding that the jurisdiction of the Magistrate to take cognizance of the complaint was not barred by Section 195(1)(b) and (c). The Court found that the offenses under Sections 167 and 466 were not covered by the statutory bar, and for the offense under Section 471, a necessary condition for the bar to apply—that the offense was committed by a party to the proceeding—was not fulfilled.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution adopted the device of not charging the appellant under Section 193 of the Penal Code with a view to evading the bar of Section 195(1)(b) of the Code.

facts: The appellant was charged under Section 167 of the Penal Code, among other sections.
The appellant argued that the facts of the case actually constituted an offense under Section 193 of the Penal Code.

The appellant contended that the prosecution deliberately chose to charge them under Section 167 to avoid the procedural bar found in Section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which would have applied to a charge under Section 193.
law: Section 195(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure creates a procedural bar, preventing a court from taking cognizance of certain offenses, including Section 193 of the Penal Code, unless a complaint is filed by the appropriate court.
This procedural bar in Section 195(1)(b) does not apply to an offense under Section 167 of the Penal Code.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had already performed a "careful analysis" and "very elaborate consideration" of the allegations and materials in the case.
The High Court had compared the legal ingredients of the offenses under Sections 192, 193, and 167 of the Penal Code.
Based on this analysis, the High Court concluded that the charge framed against the appellant under Section 167 was justified by the facts of the case.
The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention. It held that since the High Court had justifiably found that the charge under Section 167 was appropriate based on the facts, it could not be considered a mere "device" to evade the procedural bar. Because the charge was properly framed under Section 167, a section to which the bar in Section 195(1)(b) does not apply, the court had the jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offense.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be considered a "party to any proceeding in any Court" for the purpose of invoking the bar under Section 195(1)(c) of the Code.

facts: The appellant was a magistrate against whom transfer applications were filed to move cases from his court.
These transfer applications contained allegations against the appellant, and he was asked to submit a report on them.
The appellant was subsequently charged with offenses including one under Section 471 of the Penal Code (using a forged document).
law: Section 195(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, creates a bar on a court taking cognizance of certain offenses, including an offense under Section 471 of the Penal Code.
For this bar to apply, the offense must be alleged to have been committed "by a party to any proceeding in any Court."
application: The appellant argued that he should be considered a party to the transfer application proceedings because allegations were made against him and he was involved in the process.
The Supreme Court rejected this argument, stating that merely being the subject of allegations in transfer applications does not make a magistrate a "party" to those proceedings.
The Court reasoned that the appellant was acting in his official capacity as a magistrate and had no personal interest in the outcome of the transfer applications.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant could not be characterized as a "party to any proceeding in any Court" within the meaning of Section 195(1)(c). Consequently, the bar under that section did not apply, and the court was not prevented from taking cognizance of the offense.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were applicable and should have been complied with before the prosecution was initiated.

facts: The appellant argued that the prosecution against him was illegal because the mandatory provisions of Section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed.
Specifically, the appellant contended that the complaint should have been filed by the Additional District Magistrate (ADM) after conducting a proper inquiry as required by the section.
law: Section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure outlines the procedure for a court to file a complaint regarding certain offences committed in or in relation to a proceeding before it.
The application of Section 476 is linked to the offences and circumstances described in Section 195(1)(b) and (c) of the Code.
application: The Court provided two main reasons for rejecting the appellant's argument.

First, the Court had already determined that the provisions of Section 195(1)(b) or (c) did not apply to the appellant's case. The Court stated that this finding was, by itself, "enough to hold that Section 476 of the Code does not come into picture," as the applicability of Section 476 is dependent on Section 195.

Second, the Court held that even if Section 195 were applicable, the facts did not support the application of Section 476. While it might have appeared that the ADM was conducting a preliminary inquiry under Section 476, a review of his order showed otherwise. The findings recorded against the appellant were merely the reasons for transferring the cases from the appellant's file. The ADM himself did not take any action contemplated by Section 476, such as filing a complaint; he only forwarded a copy of his order to the State Government to consider sanctioning action.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention that Section 476 should have been complied with. It concluded that the section was not applicable, primarily because its prerequisite (the applicability of Section 195) was not met, and secondarily, because the actions of the Additional District Magistrate did not constitute an inquiry or action under Section 476.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint failed to disclose the commission of any offence.

facts: The appellant's counsel contended that the complaint filed against the appellant did not disclose the commission of any offence.
The complaint alleged that the appellant had made interpolations and forgeries in judicial records, framed incorrect documents with intent to cause injury, and used forged documents as genuine.
law: The standard for a complaint to be valid is whether the allegations within it disclose the commission of an offence, not whether the accused is ultimately guilty.
application: The Court examined the allegations in the complaint, which included forgery and interpolation of judicial records.
It determined that these allegations were sufficient to disclose the offences alleged against the appellant, which required a Magistrate to take cognizance of the case.
The Court explicitly separated the issue of whether the complaint disclosed an offence from the ultimate question of the appellant's guilt or innocence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found the contention to be "absolutely devoid of any merit," holding that the allegations in the complaint did disclose the commission of offences. Therefore, the Court rejected the argument.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The procedural bar to a court taking cognizance of an offence, as stipulated in Section 195(1)(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, does not apply to prosecutions for offences under Section 167 and Section 466 of the Indian Penal Code.
obiter: Any observations made in this judgment agreeing with the views expressed by the High Court are only for the purpose of dealing with the contentions raised on behalf of the appellant.
The point of time at which the legality of the cognizance taken is to be adjudged is the time when cognizance is actually taken under Section 190 of the Code.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that none of the procedural bars raised by the appellant under the Code of Criminal Procedure were applicable to this case. The jurisdiction of the Magistrate to take cognizance of the complaint was not barred by Section 195(1)(b) or (c) because the primary offences charged, Sections 167 and 466 of the Penal Code, are not covered by those provisions. For the offence under Section 471 of the Penal Code, which is mentioned in Section 195(1)(c), the bar did not apply because the appellant, a Magistrate, was not a 'party' to the transfer proceedings in which the allegations against him were made. Consequently, as the bar under Section 195 did not apply, the procedural requirements of Section 476 of the Code were also not triggered.
legal_tests_applied: To determine if the bar under Section 195(1)(b) or (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies, the court must first check if the specific Penal Code offence charged is listed within those clauses.

For the bar under Section 195(1)(c) to operate against an offence like Section 471 of the Penal Code, it is essential that the offence is alleged to have been committed 'by a party to any proceeding in any Court'.

To determine if a judicial officer is a 'party' to a proceeding for the purposes of Section 195(1)(c), the court assesses whether the officer has a personal interest in the outcome of the proceeding, as distinct from their official function as a Magistrate.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the prosecution was barred by Section 195(1)(b) and (c) failed because the specific offences for which he was committed—Sections 167 and 466 of the Penal Code—are not covered by those clauses.

The court rejected the contention that the prosecution deliberately charged the appellant under Section 167 to evade the bar applicable to Section 193, accepting the High Court's finding that the charge under Section 167 was justified by the facts and materials of the case.

The appellant's claim to be a 'party' to the transfer proceedings, which would invoke the bar of Section 195(1)(c) for the Section 471 charge, was dismissed. The court reasoned: 'Merely on the basis that the applications for transfer of certain cases pending before the appellant had been filed making allegation against the appellant will not -make the appellant a party to those proceedings. He was functioning as a Magistraie and he has no personal interest in the outcome of the transfer applications.'

The argument that the mandatory provisions of Section 476 of the Code were violated was rejected because the applicability of Section 476 is predicated on the bar under Section 195(1)(b) or (c) applying. Since those sections did not apply, 'it follows that Section 476 of the Code also has .no application.'

The contention that the complaint failed to disclose the commission of any offence was summarily rejected by the court, which stated, 'it. cannot be said that no offence is disclosed in the complaint. This contention is also rejected.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded because the court agreed that the specific charges framed against the appellant were not subject to the procedural bar on cognizance. The court explicitly stated: 'The offence under Section 466 of the Penal Code is, admittedly, not covered by Clause (b) or Clause (c) of Section 195 (I) of the Code.' and 'As the charge has been framed under Section 167, the bar under Section 195 (1) (b) or (c) of the Code bas no application.'

The prosecution's choice of charges was deemed legitimate and not a device to evade procedural hurdles, as the court agreed with the High Court's 'careful analysis' that the charge under Section 167 was justified.

The respondent's position that the appellant was not a 'party' for the purpose of Section 195(1)(c) was upheld. The court found the appellant was merely functioning in his official capacity as a Magistrate and lacked the personal interest required to be considered a party to the transfer applications.
As a direct consequence of the inapplicability of Section 195, the respondent's position that Section 476 did not need to be complied with was affirmed by the court.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning distinguishes between a judicial officer's official role and their status as a private litigant. By holding that a Magistrate against whom allegations are made in a transfer application is not a 'party' because he has 'no personal interest in the outcome,' the court protects judicial officers from being drawn into litigation as parties simply for actions taken or allegations made in the course of their official duties.

The judgment implicitly reinforces the proper internal judicial hierarchy for addressing complaints against judicial officers. The court noted that when allegations are made, it is the officer's 'duty as a subordinate court... to offer explanations in his report sent to by his superior,' suggesting this is the appropriate channel rather than treating the officer as a party to the proceeding itself.
